full_judgment:
Md Nazrul Islam Talukder J : This Rule was issued on an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the proceeding of Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 4507 of 2009 arising out of CR Case No. 663 of 2009 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 now pending before the Court of Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The prosecution case, in short, is that the accused-petitioner approached opposite party No. 2 for taking personal loan for business purpose. Opposite party No. 2 agreed to provide personal loan for the aforesaid purposes. Accordingly, an agreement was executed and signed by the parties on 21-11-2007. Based on the said agreement the accused-petitioner borrowed Taka 1,00,00,000 (one crore) only from opposite party No. 2. In view of terms and conditions of the agreement, the petitioner agreed to pay Taka 28,00,000 (twenty eight lakh) only as profit to opposite party No. 2 per year. Pursuant to the accused-petitioner issued two cheques bearing Nos. 6874801 and 6474802 dated 21-11-2008 for payment of Taka 28,00,000 (twenty eight lakh) only per year as a yearly profit. On 27-11-2008, opposite party No. 2 presented one of the aforesaid cheques bearing No. 6874801 dated 21-11-2008 to Standard Chartered Bank for encashment but that cheque was bounced because of insufficient fund on 27-11-2008. Finding no other way, opposite party No. 2 issued a legal notice upon the petitioner on 7-12-2008 requesting him to pay the said amount of money. On receipt of the legal notice on 11-12-2008, the petitioner promised to pay the money within 30-4-2009 but he did not pay the same within the stipulated time. Opposite party No. 2, thereafter, filed a petition of complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (herein after referred to as the Act) before the Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, Dhaka after complying with all necessary formalities as required by laws and the same was registered as CR Case No. 663 of 2009. 

 3. The Metropolitan Magistrate, by an order dated 12-2-2009, took cognizance of the offence against the accused-petitioner under section 138 of the Act. Subsequently, the Metropolitan Magistrate sent the record of the case to the Court of learned Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka who sent the case to the Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka for trial and the case was, subsequently, numbered as Metropolitan Sessions Case No. 4507 of 2009 and the date for framing charge was fixed on 2-2-2010. 

 4. On the date of framing charge, the accused petitioner submitted an application under section 265C of the Code of Criminal Procedure for discharging him the case. The learned Judge of the trial Court rejected the application filed by the petitioner and framed charge against him under section 138 of the Act, on 2-2-2010. 

 6. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, learned Advocate along with Mr Dr Ataul H Khan Alamgir, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the allegations which have been brought against the petitioner are purely a business dispute and that as per clause 6 of the agreement dated 21-11-2007 executed and signed between the parties, such dispute should strictly be settled through the arbitration under the Salish AM, 2001. He further submits that the proceeding under section 138 of the Act is not maintainable as opposite party No. 2 has already filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 2009 under section 12 of the Salish Ain, 2001 and that arbitrators were appointed by the learned District Judge. He emphatically submits that no Court is empowered to entertain any legal proceeding in respect of the selfsame matter under section 7 of the Salish Ain, 2001 as well as under section 138 of the Act. He next submits that since the cheque is the part and parcel of the agreement and that since opposite party No. 2 has accepted the terms and conditions of the agreement, any dispute arising out of the cheque must be settled by arbitration as per clause 6 as stipulated in the agreement and, as such, the impugned proceeding is nothing but an abuse of process of the Court and, as such, the impugned proceeding may be quashed. He lastly submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court has totally failed to appreciate section 265(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and that the decision in the case of Manzur Alam vs State, 55 DLR (AD) 62 cited by opposite party No. 2 has no manner of application in the instant case and, as such, the impugned proceeding may be quashed. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr Tanjib-ul-Alam along with Mr Imtiaz Mahmood and Mr Mahfuz Bin Yousuf, learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 2, submits that the offence under section 138 of the Act is an independent criminal offence and that the proceeding under section 138 of the Act, 1881 is completely an independent criminal proceeding which shall continue notwithstanding the pendency of arbitration proceeding which shall continue notwithstanding the pendency of arbitration proceeding which is civil in nature. He further submits that admittedly, the accused-petitioner issued a cheque in favour of opposite party No. 2 who, in due course, presented the cheque to the concerned Bank for encashment but the same was bounced for insufficient fund and that the accused-petitioner did not make any payment within the stipulated time after receipt of a legal notice and that a civil suit and a criminal case over the selfsame matter can run together. In support of his submissions, he relied upon the decision in the case of Manzur Alam vs State, 55 DLR (AD) 62. He next submits that the purpose of arbitration and Criminal proceeding is quite different and distinguishable from each other and that a criminal proceeding cannot be prevented notwithstanding the fact that the agreement contains arbitration clause to settled the dispute arising out of the cheque. In support of his contention, he relied upon the decision in the case of SW Planitkar vs State of Bihar, (2002) 1 SCC 241. He emphatically submits that at the time of framing charge, the learned Judge of the trial Court will consider the materials of the prosecution and not of the defence and that the learned Judge of the trial Court has rightly framed charge against the accused-petitioner on the basis of materials available on record. In support of his contention, he relied upon the decision in the case of Md Moudud Ahmed vs State 1996 BLD (AD) 27 = 48 DLR (AD) 42. He lastly submits that according to section 10(1) of the Arbitration Act, 2001, there is a provision for filing written statement by the parties but in a criminal Proceeding, there is no provision for filing written statement and, as such, the arbitration proceeding is, obviously, civil in nature and, as such, initiation of arbitration proceeding between the parties does not preclude the aggrieved person from filing a proceeding under section 138 of the Act and, as such, the Rule may be discharged. 

 8. It appears form counter affidavit that opposite party No. 2 filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 2009 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka in respect of cheque No. 6874802 dated 21-11-2009 and cheque No. 6874803 dated 21-11-2009 issued by the accused petitioner. After receiving the case the learned District Judge appointed arbitrators. During pendency of Arbitration Miscellaneous Case, opposite party No. 2 filed CR Case No. 266 of 2010 in respect of cheque No. 6874802 dated 21-11-2009 and also filed CR Case No. 267 of 2010 in respect of cheque No. 6874803 dated 21-11-2009. Though opposite party No. 2 filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 2009, he, during pendency of aforesaid arbitration proceeding, produced the aforesaid cheques before the concerned Bank for encashment but those were bounced owing to lack of necessary deposit. 

 9. Accordingly, CR Case No. 266 of 2010 and CR Case No. 267 of 2010 were filed by opposite party No. 2 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka after observing all formalities required under the Act. During pendency of the said Criminal Cases, the accused petitioner filed an application in the arbitration proceeding before the learned District Judge praying for maintaining status quo in respect of said cheques and he also filed another application for stay of all further proceedings of the said two criminal proceeding in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 2009. The learned District Judge allowed both the applications and stayed all further proceedings of CR Case No. 266 of 2010 and CR Case No. 267 of 2010 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and directed both the parties to maintain status-quo in respect of cheque Nos. 6874802 and 6874803 dated 21-11-2009 issued by the accused-petitioner. 

 10. Being aggrieved by order No. 13 dated 3-2-2010 passed in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 205 of 2009, opposite party No. 2 filed Revision No. 1059 of 2010 before this Court which, by the judgment and order dated 9-8-2010, made the Rule Absolute after setting aside the impugned order dated 3-2-2010. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order, the accused-petitioner filed Civil Miscellaneous Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 685 of 2010 before the Appellate Division but the learned Judge in Chamber did not pass any order of stay. From the discussion made above, it transpires that the dispute arose between the parties in respect of the aforesaid two dishonoured cheques. 

 11. However, the subject matter of the present case is not same with the aforementioned cases. The present case arises out of a dishonoured cheque No. 6874801 dated 21-11-2008 which is different from the aforesaid cheques. No arbitration proceeding has been filed in respect of cheques No. 6874801 dated 21-11-2008. 

 12. We have gone through the application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, counter affidavit filed by opposite party No. 2, reply to counter-affidavit filed by the accused-petitioner and the materials annexed thereto. We have also considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates for both the sides. It appears from the petition of complaint that the accused-petitioner issued a cheque bearing No. 6874801 dated 21-11-2008 which was presented before the concerned Bank for encashment but that cheque was dishonoured. Opposite party No. 2 issued legal notice upon the accused-petitioner who did not make any payment against the cheque issued by him. Opposite party No. 2, thereafter, filed CR Case No. 663 of 2009 under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 after observing all legal formalities required under sections 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 13. We have considered the relevant provision of law contemplated in sections 7/9/10/ 17 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure to determine whether arbitration miscellaneous proceeding is a civil matter or not. Sub-section (1) of section 10 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 provides that any party to a legal proceedings may, at any time before filing a written statement applied to the Court before which the proceedings are pending to refer the matter to arbitration. There is no such provision of filing written statement in a criminal proceeding. In the case of Md Yousuf vs Alhaj GP Mollah, 1987 BLD 77, it has been spelt out that "all disputes between the parties relating to private rights or obligations which the civil Court may take cognizance under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure may be referred to arbitration". Considering the proposition of law and the decision mentioned above, we are of the view that the Arbitration Miscellaneous case is, no doubt, a civil proceeding. 

 14. Now we want to discuss if an offence under section 138 of the Act has been, prima-facie, committed by the accused-petitioner or not. In the case of Manzur Alam vs State, 55 DLR (AD) 62, it is held that under section 138 of the Act an offence is committed if a cheque is dishonoured and if the payment is not made within the stipulated time after receipt of a legal notice and criminal proceeding may be proceeded independently of the civil suit. In the case of PW Palanitkar vs State of Bihar, (2002) 1 SCC 241, it has been held that "for the alleged breach of the agreement in relation to commercial transaction, it is open to respondent No. 2 to proceed against the appellants for his redress for recovery of money by way of damages for the loss caused, if any. Merely because there is an arbitration clause in the agreement, that cannot prevent criminal prosecution against the accused if an act constituting a criminal offence is made out even prima facie". On close perusal of the petition of complaint, it appears to us that a clear and definite prima-facie case has been made out under section 138 of the Act to proceed against the petitioner and opposite party No. 2 has filed the petition of complaint after complying with the provisions of laws required under section 138 and 141 of the Act. 

 15. In the case of Md Moudud Ahmed vs State 1996 BLD (AD) 27 = 48 DLR (AD) 42 it has been settled that "while framing charge the trial Court is only to see if on the basis of materials on record a prima-facie case to go for the trial has been made out against the accused persons". In the instant case, there is an agreement between the parties and admittedly a cheque was issued by the accused petitioner but the same was bounced for lack of insufficient fund. In view of above facts and laws, we find the learned Judge of the trial Court rightly framed charge against the petitioner under section 138 of the Act. 

 16. In the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 38, it has been spelt out that to bring a case within the purview of section 561A of the code of criminal procedure for the purpose of quashing a proceeding one of the following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 (1) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused. 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FIR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged. 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 17. Similar view on the categories of cases for quashing the proceedings was, subsequently, reflected in the decisions in the cases of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 1997 BLD (AD) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16 and Sher Ali vs State 46 DLR (AD) 67. The present case does not come within the ambit of the principles of quashing the proceedings as the petition of complaint of the present case disclose prima-facie case against the petitioner under section 138 of the Act. 

 18. Considering the allegations made in the petition of complaint and the settled ratio discussed above, we are of the view that prima facie, criminal offence has been committed by the petitioner under section 138 of the Act and that there is no legal bar in filing a criminal case for criminal liability before the Court having jurisdiction notwithstanding the fact that a civil suit is pending over a self same matter. An aggrieved person cannot be precluded from filing a criminal case if criminal offence is committed in spite of the fact that there is an arbitration clause in an agreement made between the parties. The purpose of arbitration proceeding and criminal proceeding is quite different and distinguishable from each other. Arbitration proceeding entails various claims including recovery of money by way of damages for the loss caused by cheque or cheques and issues relating to private rights or obligations which the civil Court may take cognizance under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On the other hand, criminal proceeding relates to and arises out of an act committing a criminal offence. Both the criminal case and the arbitration proceeding can run at the same time and, as such, initiation and continuation of the criminal proceeding in a criminal Court having jurisdiction is maintainable. Having considered all aspects of the case, we do not find any merit in this Rule. 

 21. The learned Judge of the trial Court is hereby directed to dispose of the case as expeditiously as possible preferably within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of a copy of this judgment.
